phrases.text: A five-day job, six hours from home.
Two ways to run it.
The flow in this video, and the way HBCField works today.
In their flow, the technician taps Start, and a timer counts the drive.
On site, he clocks in and out on the task itself, every day.
After each clock-out, a daily report is required before he can clock in again.
On Friday he finishes, types the drive home from memory, and the customer signs the whole week at the end.
It reads well. But on a real week it breaks in four places.
One. The clock lives on the task, so two jobs in one day need a special rule.
Two. The drive home is typed by hand, so it is a guess.
Three. A missing report blocks the next clock-in, and the work stops.
Four. One technician. A crew of three has no place in it.
HBCField starts from the person, not the task.
You clock in once, for your day. Every job you touch counts inside that shift.
On the way records the real route on the map, kilometre by kilometre, not just a timer.
Clock out, and the job pauses by itself, with a handover note for whoever comes next.
And a crew shares one job, each person with their own time, and one leader.
Side by side.
Travel: a timer, against a real GPS route.
The clock: tied to one task, against one shift for any number of jobs.
Teams: one person, against a crew with a leader.
Same goal. HBCField simply measures more, and asks the worker for less.
Their flow does have good ideas. So we take them, and make them smarter.
First, the job shows its days. Day one to day five, with hours and a note on each.
Second, the daily report moves into the clock-out sheet: work done, faults, parts, photos. Asked for, never blocking.
Third, Heading home. One tap, and the drive back is measured by GPS, like the drive out.
Fourth, one summary. Out, work, back, and the total.
And last, the customer can sign each day or at the end, and the signed report is emailed automatically.
A long job, measured the way it really happened.
HBCField.
